books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Figures from the Provost Marshal General’s report, as summarized in the 1956 report Veterans in Our Society (U.S. Government Printing Office). Figures are rounded.
stimulus.text:
Results of the four drafts under the Enrollment Act of 1863.

| Outcome | Men |
| Names drawn | 776,829 |
| Men who furnished substitutes | 73,607 |
| Men who paid $300 commutation | 86,724 |
| Men exempted | 315,509 |
| Men who failed to report | 161,244 |
| Men who entered the army as draftees | 46,347 |

Altogether 119,954 men entered the army under the act: 46,347 draftees plus 73,607 hired substitutes. The rows overlap, so they do not add to the total drawn.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table shows 776,829 names drawn but only 46,347 men entering the army as draftees. The draft’s main effect was therefore to

rationales.A: Background: only 46,347 of the 776,829 men drawn entered as draftees; volunteers filled most of the ranks.
rationales.B: Background: volunteering continued, and the draft was meant to stimulate it with bounties.
rationales.D: Background: most men drawn were exempted, paid commutation, furnished substitutes, or failed to report.
rationales.C: Only 46,347 of 776,829 men drawn entered as draftees, so the draft worked mainly by pushing men to volunteer.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the two big numbers: 776,829 drawn, 46,347 draftees.
2. That is fewer than one in sixteen.
3. The rest escaped service by substitutes, commutation, exemption, or not reporting.
4. The draft was a prod, not a net: it pushed men to volunteer before their names came up.
Remember: a law’s numbers tell you what it really did, not what its name promises.
